analysis.one_liner: Charges the biggest fossil fuel companies a share of $1 trillion, based on their past emissions, to fund climate disaster recovery and resilience.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced September 12, 2024, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and left there when the Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require each company responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel extraction or refining between 2000 and 2022 to pay a share of a $1 trillion assessment, proportional to its emissions. The money would go into a dedicated federal fund for climate disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and adaptation, with 40 percent reserved for communities hit hardest by pollution and climate impacts. Companies could pay in nine annual installments, and the bill explicitly leaves all existing lawsuits against polluters untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by climate disasters, especially low-income communities, communities of color, and Tribal and Indigenous communities: the fund must direct at least $15 billion a year to FEMA disaster response and resilience programs and $6 billion a year to Clean Air Act climate grants, with 40 percent of annual spending required to benefit environmental justice communities. Taxpayers also benefit in the sense that disaster and adaptation costs now covered by the general Treasury would be paid from a charge on the companies whose products caused the emissions.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated Polluters Pay Climate Fund filled by the assessment on large fossil fuel companies, available for climate resilience, adaptation, disaster response, and environmental justice spending [S2].

Requires at least $15 billion a year to FEMA for climate disaster response and resilience, including $3 billion for the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program, plus at least $6 billion a year in climate grants under the Clean Air Act [S2].

Sets aside 40 percent of annual fund spending for investments benefiting environmental justice communities, defined as communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities facing disproportionate pollution and climate harms [S2].

Leaves all existing legal remedies intact, so states, local governments, tribes, and individuals could still sue fossil fuel companies over climate deception and damages, and fund payments could not be used to offset court awards [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel extraction and refining companies determined to be responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2022, each owing a share of the $1 trillion proportional to its emissions above that threshold, due by September 30, 2025 or in nine annual installments. Because the charge applies to the companies' products, some of the cost could be passed along to consumers through fuel and energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large fossil fuel producers and refiners

drawbacks.text: The charge is a one-time bill for past emissions (2000-2022), not an ongoing price on future emissions, so by itself it does not reduce the greenhouse gases going into the atmosphere going forward [S2].

The bill's own findings acknowledge the $100 billion annual assessment is only a small portion of the trillions the federal response to climate change will require, so most climate costs would still fall on taxpayers even if it passed [S2].

Because the tax reaches back more than two decades and applies to conduct before enactment, affected companies would almost certainly challenge it in court, which could delay or prevent collection, and companies could pass some of the cost to consumers through higher fuel prices [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is concrete and large: a trillion dollars for disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and adaptation, aimed disproportionately at communities that have been hit hardest, without adding to the deficit and without limiting anyone's right to sue polluters. The honest costs are that it does nothing directly to cut future emissions, that fuel prices could rise somewhat as companies absorb the charge, and that retroactive collection would face years of legal challenge before money flowed. On balance it is a genuine transfer from the companies whose products caused the emissions to the people who bear the consequences, though it addresses past harm more than future prevention.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate on September 12, 2024 and sent to the Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill on September 12, 2024, joined by Senators Sanders, Warren, Markey, Merkley, and Whitehouse [S2][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in its record [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee, so no committee vote, floor vote, or House action ever took place [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The fossil fuel companies that would have owed shares of the $1 trillion assessment were spared the charge, and the cost of climate disasters and adaptation continues to fall on general taxpayers and the communities hit by those disasters.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies; disaster costs stay with taxpayers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Senator Sanders, and no Republican signed on before the bill died in committee [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Fossil fuel extraction and refining companies
industries.note: Companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of CO2 from 2000-2022 would owe a proportional share of a $1 trillion assessment, payable by 2025 or over nine installments. Their interest in avoiding the charge runs directly against the communities the fund would pay for climate recovery.

Coal extraction counts toward a company's emissions total, with fixed conversion rates determining how each million pounds of coal adds to the bill, so large coal producers would owe part of the assessment.

A one-time $1 trillion charge on producers and refiners could partly show up in gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Households would also be the beneficiaries of the disaster recovery and resilience spending the fund pays for.
